title: TDDR Rising Narratives — Monday morning, Nov 23
summary: A snapshot of opposition narratives from the Right and the Far Left as of 7:45 AM ET Monday, Nov 23, 2026. Built for TDDR (Too Dumb Didn't Read). Medicare for All is still the largest query (32,796 posts in 24 hours, 2.45× its prior daily average) as the left argues over whether El-Sayed's version is really a public option. On the Right, 'Democrats crashed the market' rose overnight (6,061 posts from 5 PM to 7 AM ET versus 2,210 a night earlier; 9,884 in 24 hours, 2.72×) after Treasury Secretary Bessent said the sell-off 'began as the Democrats moved ahead in the polls'; he also blamed a hawkish Fed, and Trump's 'Nasdaq down 20%' is still wrong. New: Fox co-host Jessica Tarlov's podcast remark that Trump's 'very fine people' line was not about neo-Nazis became 'the Charlottesville hoax' overnight (8,467 posts, almost all after 5 PM Sunday; 'Jessica Tarlov' was a U.S. trend). Also new, on the Far Left: backlash to Rahm Emanuel telling DSA-aligned members who voted against Jeffries 'I'll see you in November' (688 posts, 11.16× a tiny baseline). The forensic-audit push held (9,624 posts), Van Hollen vs. Schumer cooled slightly (11,991), and the Rikers card faded (5,763, 0.50×). Two faded cards were dropped and two were added. Every count, quote and fact-check comes from sources and X queries pulled this morning or carried over from last evening and labeled. Nothing here is invented.

'US Army' (19,567) and 'Libya' did not relate to a U.S. opposition narrative. Where a trend object had no tweet_count ('Victory Monday,' '#MondayVibes'), its volume is unavailable and we did not estimate it.

oppositionNote.body: Right = narratives the Right is pushing after the Democratic midterm wave. Far Left = pressure on Democratic leadership and the incoming majority from the party's left. The Rikers card is a Right attack on a Democratic mayor; we include it because Mamdani is being used as the national face of the party. The market card is tagged Right because the 'Democrats crashed the market' frame comes from Trump and his Treasury Secretary, even though many posts matching the query are rebuttals. The immigration card is tagged Right because the 'replacing Black voters' frame is the Right's reading of Stephen A. Smith's comments; Smith is a Democratic voter. The Rubio card recasts the incoming majority as Marxist, using a 2020 video. The Obama card is tagged Right because the backlash, not Obama's remark, is the narrative. The new 'fine people' card is tagged Right because it uses a Fox co-host's comment to brand Democrats as liars; it is about a 2017 quote, not the midterms. The new Rahm Emanuel card is tagged Far Left because the narrative is the left's backlash to a centrist Democrat, even though Emanuel's remarks also circulate on the Right as proof of a Democratic civil war. The Medicare for All card is tagged Far Left because the pressure is on Jeffries, Schumer and the incoming majority to deliver it now. The Van Hollen card is tagged Far Left because the push to replace Schumer comes from the party's left. The tag is the primary opposition frame.

methodology: Last updated Monday, Nov 23, 2026, 7:45 AM ET. This is a research snapshot for TDDR, not a live API, and it will go stale. U.S. X trends were pulled at about 7:13 AM ET. Last evening's snapshot (Nov 22, 5:20 PM ET) is kept in the archive and was not overwritten. Eight of its ten narratives were re-counted with the same queries so momentum compares like with like. The new 24-hour window overlaps last evening's by 10 hours (7 AM to 5 PM Sunday ET), so we also report each query's 5 PM–7 AM ET overnight count against the same hours a night earlier. Two narratives were dropped because they faded: the 'nullify the midterms' card (2,771 posts in the last 24 hours, 0.68× its prior daily average; 1,457 from 5 PM to 7 AM ET versus 3,029 the same hours a night earlier) and the 'third impeachment' card (1,295 posts, 0.78×; 460 versus 518). Two were added with new queries: the 'fine people hoax' and the Rahm Emanuel–DSA fight. Other candidates were counted and not carved out as cards: Florida's subpoena of DSA over alleged foreign funding (1,668 posts, 3.34×; the query also caught unrelated AI posts using 'DSA' for a model architecture, so we did not trust it); the 'Democrats will raise your taxes' card after Rep. Richard Neal's plan to revisit the 2017 tax cuts (584 posts, 0.75×); and Jeffries's Iran-funding stance (411 posts, 0.33×). Republican anger at the Senate over the stalled SAVE America Act was again covered by X News but is an intra-Republican fight, so we did not score it as an opposition narrative.

For each narrative we ran one English-language X search with x.get_posts_counts_recent twice: at daily granularity over a 167-hour window from 8:00 AM ET Monday, Nov 16, through 7:00 AM ET Monday, Nov 23 (the 'seven-day' total), and at hourly granularity over the last 24 hours (7:00 AM ET Sunday, Nov 22, through 7:00 AM ET Monday, Nov 23). We counted named news or fact-check outlets whose coverage we opened or retrieved and cite on the card. Official government pages, bill text, transcripts, advocacy groups, research groups, blogs, aggregators, X News summaries, archives and X posts are cited as sources but not counted as outlets; Page Twenty One and MarketDash are cited on the market card but not counted. This morning we researched the two new cards and re-researched the market and Van Hollen cards; the other cards carry last evening's outlet counts and say so. One topic in this set, the 'fine people' card ('Jessica Tarlov'), appeared on the U.S. trends list at about 7:13 AM ET.

Score = 50% volume index + 30% acceleration index + 20% coverage index. Volume index is 100 × log10(1 + last-24h posts) / log10(1 + the highest last-24h count in this set). Acceleration index is 100 × min(last-24h / prior daily average, 3) / 3, so a triple-or-higher average scores 100. Prior daily average is (seven-day total − last 24h) / 6. Coverage index is 70 × min(outlets, 7) / 7, plus 30 if the topic was on the U.S. X trends list this morning. The 'fine people' card got the trend bonus. The 'fine people,' Rubio, Obama and Rahm Emanuel queries had tiny baselines earlier in the week, so their acceleration indexes are maxed out. The Medicare for All and Van Hollen queries already carried large daily volumes all week, which keeps their acceleration modest. Read the post counts alongside the scores. Evening-to-morning score changes also reflect the volume ceiling (32,796 this morning versus 29,334 last evening) and how much coverage we retrieved.

Counts are query matches, not unique posts or unique users, and queries can overlap. The audit query catches posts mocking the demand. The market query requires a market term plus 'Democrats' or 'blue wave,' so it also catches rebuttals and general market posts that mention Democrats. The 'fine people' query requires 'fine people' or Charlottesville plus hoax, Tarlov, 'The Five,' Biden or context, so it also catches posts defending the original reading. The Rahm Emanuel query includes the bare name 'Rahm' and terms like 2028, so it catches news posts and Right-leaning posts about the fight. The Rikers query also catches straight news posts and rebuttals. The Medicare for All query catches supporters, opponents and general health-care posts, and its 'M4A' term can catch unrelated uses. The Van Hollen query catches syndicated news posts. The immigration query includes the phrase 'Stephen A,' so it can catch unrelated Stephen A. Smith posts. The Rubio query catches any post pairing 'democratic socialism' with Marxism or communism, including posts from other countries. The Obama query can catch unrelated golf talk. Replies are included. Sentiment is a qualitative label from relevancy-sorted post samples and from quotes in news coverage, not a scientific poll. This morning we pulled fresh samples for the 'fine people,' Rahm Emanuel, market, Medicare for All, audit and Rubio queries. The Van Hollen, Rikers, immigration and Obama cards carry last evening's sentiment and say so. Daily bar charts use UTC days (a UTC day starts at 7:00 PM ET the previous evening). Bars marked * are partial windows. Hourly charts are labeled in ET.

disinfo.caveatBody: New this morning: 'Jessica Tarlov admitted the "very fine people" hoax' gets the narrow point right and the conclusion wrong. Trump did say he was 'not talking about the neo-Nazis and the white nationalists,' and Snopes rated the claim that he called them 'very fine people' False; but Snopes also notes the Unite the Right rally was conceived, led and attended by white supremacists, so 'very fine people on both sides' was itself inaccurate, and one commentator's podcast remark is not evidence that Democrats invented the quote. Bessent's 'the sell-off began as the Democrats moved ahead in the polls' is his reading of the timing, not a measured cause; in the same answer he cited hawkish Fed remarks and tighter financial conditions (CBS News transcript), and coverage ties the drop to the AI sell-off, the Anthropic IPO and Nvidia's turmoil as well as to expected data-center rules (NPR; The Hill). Page Twenty One finds Trump's 'more than $6 trillion' roughly right on a total-market basis, 'Nasdaq down 20%' exaggerated (about 10.9% from the Nov. 3 close to Nov. 20) and '100% due to the Democrats' not supported. Carried over from last evening: Trump's 'NASDAQ, by itself, is down 20%' since the Nov. 3 midterms is wrong. From the last close before the vote (Nov. 2) to Friday's close the Nasdaq Composite fell 10.1%, the S&P 500 8.4% and the Dow 7.4% (Mediaite; MODEL, checking Nasdaq index data); the Composite is 18.1% below its Oct. 6 record, and the Nasdaq-100 is 19.8% below its record. '100% due to the Democrats' leaves out the AI and chip sell-off and the turmoil at Nvidia that coverage ties last week's drop to (The Hill), and the new Congress is not sworn in until Jan. 3, 2027. The viral Marco Rubio 'Democratic socialism… is Marxism' video is from Feb. 24, 2020, when he was a senator commenting on Bernie Sanders's primary campaign (Political Wire; The Right Scoop), not a response to this month's election. 'El-Sayed abandoned Medicare for All' is overstated: he said on Meet the Press he supports Sanders's bill but prefers a version that keeps private plans available (NBC News; POLITICO). 'Forensic-audit all 50 states before certifying' is misleading. Every state already has a post-election audit procedure (NCSL, via Votebeat), Texas began its first statewide risk-limiting audit of the U.S. Senate race on Nov. 19 (Houston Public Media), and audits and certification are separate processes that can run in parallel (The Crosscheck, which rated the 'don't certify until verified' claim Misleading). Earlier viral fraud claims, a Houston 'FBI raid' and a Wyandot County, Ohio, tally error, were debunked by PolitiFact and AFP. 'Medicare for All saves 114,000 lives and $1 trillion a year' is a projection from a Yale preprint that has not been peer reviewed; about 51,300 of those lives come from reversing coverage cuts enacted since 2025, not from single-payer itself, and the model leaves out transition costs (Yale School of Public Health; Renaissance Physician). Trump's 'Democrats Hurt Stocks' chart gets the numbers right and the cause wrong. The S&P 500 did fall 8.7% from the Nov. 3 close to the Nov. 20 close, and total U.S.-listed market value fell about $7.7 trillion (Candid Dragon's chatter check), but stocks rallied the day after the results, Friday's drop is tied mainly to the Nvidia accounting-probe report and the AI sell-off (Reuters; CNBC), and the new Congress is not sworn in until Jan. 3, 2027. 'Democrats are importing immigrants to replace Black voters' is Stephen A. Smith's stated belief, not an established fact: the census does count every resident for House seats, as the Constitution requires, but noncitizens cannot vote in federal elections (18 U.S.C. § 611), and PolitiFact has rated the related claim that millions of immigrants are registering to vote Pants on Fire. 'Trump endorsed Medicare for All' is overstated: he reposted El-Sayed's 'TrumpCare' card and praised Democrats' health-care ideas but has not backed a bill. 'Mamdani is releasing thousands of criminals' and 'Mamdani is closing Rikers now' get the plan backward: it sets a target of no more than 4,100 people in custody by the end of 2032, reached through diversion and shorter case delays, keeps Rikers open until borough jails are built, and asks the City Council to move the legal deadline later, from August 2027 to 2032 (City of New York; City & State; Gothamist). 'The Protect Our Neighbors Act gives 1.6 million people green cards' is misleading.

Trump did say there were 'very fine people on both sides' and, in the same answer, 'I'm not talking about the neo-Nazis and the white nationalists, because they should be condemned totally'; Snopes rated the claim that he called neo-Nazis 'very fine people' False in 2024, while noting that the rally was organized and attended by white supremacists.

narratives.whyItWorks: It packages a years-old argument as fresh news with a confession from the other side, which is the most shareable format in partisan media. narratives.counter: Don't relitigate the clip. The video is not new: Rubio posted it from his car on Feb. 24, 2020, about Bernie Sanders's primary run (Political Wire; The Right Scoop; The Mary Sue, all from Feb. 2020). Most sharers did not date it. X News summarized it as a 'resurfaced clip.' It lands as the Medicare for All push, Van Hollen's challenge and the 'Mamdani' Rikers story give the Right a 'socialist majority' frame. Democratic socialists are a minority within the incoming Democratic majority; the House picked Hakeem Jeffries, who does not support Medicare for All, as its nominee for speaker. talkingPoints: Democratic socialism sounds benign. It's not. It's built on Marxism.
They trade your freedom for 'free' health care, and when it fails you don't get your freedom back.
Ask a Cuban or a Venezuelan where this ends.
Medicare for All, Mamdani, Van Hollen: this is the new Democratic majority.
narratives.amplifiers: Right: @the_jefferymead (104,951 views), copy-paste reposts from smaller MAGA accounts, X News's 'Marco Rubio Warns Democratic Socialism Leads to Marxism' story. Context: @MichaelARothman dated the clip to February 2020.
narratives.whyItWorks: It is a short, calm, self-recorded clip from a sitting Secretary of State, so it reads as a warning, not a rant, and it gives a name to vague unease about a Democratic sweep. It ties a set of separate stories (Medicare for All, Mamdani, the Schumer challenge) into one frame. Because it is undated, many viewers take it as a response to this month's results.
narratives.audience: Cuban, Venezuelan and Nicaraguan American voters in Florida; older conservatives who remember the Cold War; Trump voters looking for a big-picture explanation of the midterm loss; and moderates uneasy about Medicare for All.

narratives.whyItWorks: A lifelong Democratic voter and one of the most famous Black media figures in the country gives the Right a messenger it cannot be accused of inventing, and the clip was filmed in a Black barbershop. It mixes a real grievance (Democrats taking Black loyalty for granted) and a real fact (the census counts all residents for House seats) with an unproven motive, so each step sounds reasonable. It lands three days after the Protect Our Neighbors Act gave the 'amnesty' frame a news peg.
narratives.audience: Black men who follow Smith and feel taken for granted by Democrats, immigration-restriction voters, sports-media audiences who don't follow politics closely, and Right influencers' X followings.
narratives.counter: Don't argue with Smith's frustration; agree that Democrats have to earn Black votes on prices, jobs and safety, which is what he actually asked for. Then separate the facts: noncitizens cannot vote in federal elections (18 U.S.C. § 611), and while the census does count every resident for apportionment, that rule is in the Constitution, not a Democratic plan. Smith himself says he doesn't want law-abiding, tax-paying migrants deported. On the bill: an order has to be 10 years old, the person needs 10 years of continuous presence and no serious conviction, and a judge can renew the order (bill text; ABC News).

factChecks.claim: The Protect Our Neighbors Act gives green cards to 1.6 million people with deportation orders.
factChecks.detail: The bill's sponsor puts the number of people with final removal orders at about 1.19 million; 1.6 million is an earlier ICE figure. The bill would let an order expire only after 10 years, allow a judge to renew it, and let a person petition for any status they are eligible for only after 10 years of continuous presence and no conviction for a crime punishable by more than a year. It does not hand out green cards automatically, and it has no path in the current Republican House. This is TDDR's read of the bill text and Simon's release, not a rating from a fact-check outlet.

factChecks.claim: The Protect Our Neighbors Act would wipe out 1.6 million deportation orders.
factChecks.detail: About 1.6 million people have final removal orders (ICE testimony cited by ABC News), but the bill covers only orders at least 10 years old for people continuously present with no criminal conviction, and a judge could renew an order. No count of who would qualify has been published. This is TDDR's read of that reporting, not a rating from a fact-check outlet.

narratives.whyItWorks: Crime and disorder are the Right's most reliable attack on big-city Democrats, and Mamdani is the most visible democratic socialist in office, so a jail story in New York becomes a national preview of 'Democratic rule.' Specific-sounding numbers (2,100, 2,500, 7,000) turn a six-year population target into an image of open cell doors. It also pairs with other Mamdani stories circulating Friday, such as his NYPD unit cut and his pitch for monthly DSA donations, to build a single picture.
narratives.audience: Outer-borough and suburban New Yorkers worried about crime, national conservative audiences who see Mamdani as the face of the Democratic left, and police and corrections-officer communities.
narratives.counter: Nobody is opening the doors on Friday. The plan sets a population target for the end of 2032, reached through diversion, supervised release and faster cases, and Rikers stays open until the borough jails are built (City of New York; Gothamist). Closing Rikers has been city law since 2019, passed under de Blasio; this plan actually pushes the deadline later, and it still needs City Council approval (AP). Take the real question seriously: critics doubt the target can be met safely, so answer with how many people are held on lower-level charges and how case delays will be cut, not with slogans.
